items.title: Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models and Humans on Curated AI-Generated Intraoral Images
items.abstract: Introduction and aims To evaluate the authenticity detection performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) using real and AI-generated intraoral photographs and to compare their performance with human evaluators with different levels of dental experience. Methods A dataset of 1,000 intraoral photographs (500 real and 500 AI-generated) across 5 standardised views was constructed from single-institution clinical images and the publicly available AI-Hub dataset. GPT-5.1 (OpenAI), Claude Opus 4.5 (Anthropic), and Gemini 3.0 Pro (Google) evaluated all images through vendor APIs. Human evaluation was conducted using a stratified random subset of 200 images by fourth-year dental students, dentists with ≤5 years, and dentists with ≥6 years of clinical experience (n = 5 per group). Results In the 200-image subset, dentists with ≥6 years showed the highest performance (accuracy: 0.740; F1-score: 0.675), followed by dentists with ≤5 years (accuracy: 0.690; F1-score: 0.557). Across the 1,000-image dataset, GPT-5.1 achieved the highest performance among the MLLMs (accuracy: 0.646; F1-score: 0.452), whereas Claude Opus 4.5 showed the lowest (accuracy: 0.571; F1-score: 0.249). All groups demonstrated substantially higher accuracy for real images than for the curated, visually plausible AI-generated images, with the MLLMs combining near-perfect specificity (0.998-1.000) and low recall (0.142-0.292), whereas human specificity was 0.890-0.990 and recall 0.390-0.540. The mandibular occlusal view showed the lowest accuracy among the MLLM groups. Conclusion Current MLLMs showed lower performance than experienced human evaluator panels, with limited recall for the AI-generated images in this study, suggesting that they are not yet suitable as standalone authenticity detection tools in dentistry. Clinical Relevance The increasing visual realism of generative artificial intelligence-generated intraoral photographs suggests that authenticity cannot be judged from visual inspection alone, and robust validation is needed before such images are used as clinical records, teaching material, or training data for artificial intelligence.

items.title: Performing Trust in AI-Generated Journalism: Transparency, Authorship and Accountability in Algorithmic News Content
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in news production, journalistic credibility can no longer be understood only through audience trust in machine-generated content. This article examines how AI-generated and AI-assisted journalism is made to appear trustworthy through textual, editorial, and institutional cues. Drawing on qualitative comparative content analysis of a 37-text corpus comprising 14 AI-generated or AI-assisted news articles, 14 human-written comparison articles, four newsroom AI policy documents, and five correction or controversy-related texts, the study analyses how credibility is constructed through authorship, disclosure, sourcing, human oversight, correction practice, and institutional framing. The findings show that AI-assisted journalism can reproduce familiar signs of professional news, including factual tone, structured formats, institutional attribution, and data specificity. Yet these cues do not necessarily make editorial responsibility visible. The article develops the concept of algorithmic credibility performance to explain how AI journalism assembles trustworthiness through uneven arrangements of transparency, evidence, and accountability before audiences respond.

items.title: Peripheral Inflammatory Indices in Major Depressive Disorder: Clinical Associations and Explainable Machine Learning
items.abstract: Background: The clinical relevance of routinely available peripheral inflammatory indices in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains uncertain, particularly regarding recent suicide attempts, depressive symptom severity, and their discriminative performance. This study investigated these associations using conventional statistical analyses and explainable machine learning. Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included 86 patients with MDD and 80 healthy controls. Six blood-derived inflammatory indices were examined for between-group differences and associations with recent suicide attempts and depressive symptom severity. Individual-marker discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, while three ensemble machine-learning models were evaluated using nested cross-validation and compared with MHR alone. Explainable artificial intelligence methods were applied to interpret model predictions. Results: Patients with MDD showed higher MHR, NHR, SIRI, and AISI values than controls. Recent suicide attempts were associated with higher SII, SIRI, and AISI, and these associations persisted after adjustment for age and sex; lower LHR was observed only in the unadjusted comparison and was not significant after adjustment. No inflammatory index was significantly associated with depressive symptom severity. MHR demonstrated the strongest individual discrimination. Machine-learning models showed modest discriminative performance without clear improvement over MHR alone, and feature-importance analyses consistently highlighted MHR. Conclusions: Here we show that peripheral inflammatory indices exhibit distinct observational associations with MDD and recent suicidal behavior. However, their diagnostic and predictive clinical utility remains unestablished and requires prospective, adequately controlled, independently validated studies.

items.title: Persistent Records Without Decoding Support: When a Record Survives and Its Reading Does Not
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Persistent Records Without Decoding Support, a mechanism by which a record outlasts the conventions, skills, or equipment needed to read it. The paper distinguishes two requirements for practical access. Recoverability concerns whether a reader can extract the marks or data. Intelligibility concerns whether the reader can establish what they mean. Each depends on the support available to a particular reader at a particular time. The documented case is the decipherment of Linear B. Clay tablets from Knossos and Pylos preserved palace accounts for more than 3,000 years. Before decipherment, scholars could copy the signs and recognize some pictured objects while the words beside them remained unreadable. Building on work by Alice Kober and Emmett Bennett, Michael Ventris identified the language as an early form of Greek in 1952. A tablet discovered later at Pylos helped confirm the reading. The words for two tripods appeared beside a tripod sign and the numeral 2. The 1986 BBC Domesday Project provides a contrast. By 2002, few working systems could read its videodiscs. A surviving drive supplied data for the CAMiLEON emulation demonstration, and preservation teams carried material onto newer systems. Access had become precarious while the means of reading still existed. The paper places this case alongside Jeff Rothenberg’s account of digital obsolescence and his proposal to emulate older computers. Part of the Records and Circulation series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a distinction relevant to human–AI interaction. An archive might preserve an AI system’s responses as sequences of token IDs. A later reader could copy every number, yet recovering the wording would depend on finding or reconstructing the mapping from those numbers to text.

items.title: Perspectives on the ‘human factor’ in the development of prison leavers’ digital literacy
items.abstract: This article presents findings from the evaluation of a digital literacy pilot programme for men leaving prison Tech4PrisonLeavers. It has been recognised that people leaving prison may need digital skills to support their reintegration into society. The literature on technology and digital skills programmes in the criminal justice system has largely focused on digital elements rather than human and interpersonal elements.Based on interviews with programme volunteers and coordinators, this article argues that the human factor is a key element in digital literacy programmes for prison leavers. While the digital elements of the pilot were pivotal too, the human factor represented in this case by the volunteer mentors, the volunteer-participant relationship, and associated person-centred approaches is central to supporting prison leavers’ digital needs. These interactions may ultimately lead to a two-way humanisation process in which mentors debunk prison stereotypes and the participants demystify professionals and the digital world.

items.title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.

items.title: Plug-and-Play Multi-Licensee Robust Watermarking for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
items.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable high-capacity large language models (LLMs) with high sparse computation, making them attractive for deployment on private hardware. However, distributing model weights exposes valuable intellectual property (IP) to leakage and unauthorized redistribution, creating an urgent need to both verify model ownership and trace leaked copies to individual licensees. Existing model-watermarking techniques are ill-suited for meeting this need because they are fragile under MoE's dynamic routing or require costly retraining to embed a distinct watermark for each licensee, thus making scalable distribution difficult. To address these challenges, we present PPMoE, the first plug-and-play multi-licensee watermarking framework for MoE LLMs. Rather than training a separate model per user, PPMoE trains a compact set of mergeable incremental weight modules that steer the MoE router toward distinct, mutually compatible routing patterns. During model distribution, the model owner selectively merges unique combinations of these pre-trained, mutually compatible modules into the base model on the fly, embedding a licensee-specific watermark without additional training. PPMoE supports reliable multi-licensee attribution under both white- and black-box threat models. In the white-box setting, attribution is done by inspecting triggered routing decisions or the merged weight modules responsible for these decisions, whereas in the black-box setting, attribution relies on analyzing output token likelihood ratios. Extensive experiments across five state-of-the-art MoE models, seven benchmark datasets, and varying number of licensees show that PPMoE achieves very high attribution accuracy while preserving base model utility and maintaining strong robustness to various adaptive watermark-removal attacks.

items.title: Polymorph: Operating System Kernel Optimization Through Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: While popular operating systems such as Linux and Windows were originally designed as monolithic kernels, an increasing number of kernel subsystems have become extensible using eBPF. Users can now define custom policies for essential kernel mechanisms, such as the process scheduler, page cache, and network stack, without recompiling the kernel. These mechanisms give developers significant freedom to fit the kernel to their applications' workloads, but the question of which policy to deploy remains open. We study how to use agentic AI to automate kernel policy development, selection, and deployment, focusing on the page cache and the process scheduler as two representative subsystems. We show that existing approaches fall short: evolutionary and agentic search runs offline, is relatively expensive, and often fails to generalize to online workloads, while online knob tuners are encumbered by the knobs' lack of expressivity. In contrast, we propose Polymorph, which learns online: an AI agent writes a generalized, granular policy once, and a user mode tuner adjusts its parameters during runtime, with no LLM in the loop. For the page cache, Polymorph improves throughput over Linux's LRU by 8.4% on unseen data, nearly twice the gain of the best existing policy, while adapting to workload changes at runtime and costing only 16M tokens once, versus 125-240M tokens per workload for agentic offline search. For the process scheduler, it improves on Linux's default by 2.75x across six workloads, versus 2.27x for the best fixed sched_ext policy.

items.title: Predicting Dynamic Modulus of Asphalt Mixtures Using Explainable Artificial Intelligence Techniques: A Design Optimization Application
items.abstract: Abstract Dynamic Modulus (DM) is a critical characteristic for the design of Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA), which is currently determined through complex empirical models. This study applies advanced explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques to predict DM, enhance the understanding of the factors affecting it, and support design optimization applications. An extensive experimental dataset was used that included a variety of aggregate gradations, different types of bituminous binders, volumetric characteristics, and test conditions in terms of test temperature and loading rate. Eight different predictive models were developed, ranging from simple linear regression to advanced machine learning models, including Support Vector Machines (SVM) and ensemble techniques, using a random selection scheme for cross-validation. Comparison of model performance indicated that the best performing model was the Cubic SVM, with an R 2 = 0.96 and RMSE = 2.22 × 10 5 psi, representing an approximate 39% reduction in error compared to the baseline linear regression. Explainable AI analysis revealed that phase angle was the most significant parameter in predicting DM, followed by aggregate gradation and binder characteristics. Overall, the findings show that the DM of HMA is influenced by complex nonlinear interactions among multiple factors. The AI-based models provided higher predictive accuracy and insights into interactions among material properties, supporting the development of optimized asphalt mix design guidelines for durable pavements.

items.title: Predicting Process-Level Behavior: A Benchmarking Study
items.abstract: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) typically forecasts the future of individual process instances, hence operating on trace level. Process managers, however, typically operate on process level, e.g., when assigning staff or calculating KPIs. The question is how well such process-level managerial decisions are supported by existing approaches, given that PPM research has so far not focused on process-level predictions. We answer this question through a comprehensive benchmarking study of two process-level prediction tasks: concurrent trace prediction and average throughput time prediction. Across synthetic and real-life event logs, we compare statistical and machine-learning-based methods, foundation models, business process simulation, and, importantly, established trace-level PPM approaches, aggregating their predictions to the process-level. We assess which modeling paradigms are most suitable for predicting process-level behavior and whether existing trace-level PPM can be effectively repurposed for this task. Our results show substantial variation in performance across approaches. Notably, aggregated trace-level predictions cause errors to compound on process-level, reducing accuracy and highlighting process-level prediction as a distinct predictive task that warrants dedicated research.

items.title: Predictive performance of artificial intelligence and machine learning for mosquito vector surveillance worldwide: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background Mosquito-borne diseases remain a major global public health challenge, with expanding geographic distribution driven by climate change, urbanization, and environmental modifications. Accurate forecasting of mosquito vector populations is essential for effective surveillance and control. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) approaches have emerged as promising tools for modelling complex, nonlinear relationships in vector ecology. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the predictive performance of AI and ML models applied to mosquito vector surveillance worldwide and to summarize comparative evidence with traditional statistical methods where directly reported. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive search of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus was conducted up to August 2025. Studies modelling mosquito vectors (Aedes, Culex, Anopheles) using AI/ML techniques were included. Data on study characteristics, modelling approaches, predictors, and performance metrics (e.g., AUC, sensitivity, specificity, RMSE, R 2 ) were extracted. Results were primarily synthesized descriptively because of substantial methodological and clinical/ecological heterogeneity. Exploratory random-effects meta-analyses were conducted for commonly reported performance metrics, with pooled estimates interpreted alongside measures of between-study heterogeneity and prediction intervals. Risk of bias was assessed using a PROBAST-informed assessment adapted to the ecological and entomological context. Results Seventy-one studies were included, spanning diverse geographic regions and ecological settings. Random Forest was the most frequently used algorithm. Reported predictive performance varied substantially across studies and prediction tasks, with AUC values ranging from 0.61 to 0.99. Exploratory quantitative syntheses showed exceptionally high between-study heterogeneity, limiting the generalizability of pooled performance estimates. Most studies relied on internal validation, with limited use of external validation, further limiting assessment of model performance across independent surveillance settings. Conclusions AI and ML approaches show potential for supporting mosquito vector surveillance, but reported predictive performance varies substantially across prediction tasks, taxa, ecological settings, and validation frameworks. The extreme heterogeneity observed across studies limits the generalizability of pooled performance estimates and precludes broad conclusions regarding the predictive performance of AI/ML approaches across surveillance settings. Methodological standardization, transparent reporting, external validation across independent settings, and direct comparisons with conventional statistical approaches are needed to establish the reliability and real-world applicability of these models. items.title: PReMind: When Personal Memory Meets Visual Hazards
items.abstract: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.

items.title: Preservation of Reopening Conditions Through Provisional Closure: How an Inquiry Can Stop With a Route Back
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Preservation of Reopening Conditions Through Provisional Closure, an account of how inquiry can end for the purposes of action while retaining a planned route for later reopening. The mechanism consists in preserving an unresolved dependency, a condition that would warrant reconsideration, and an accessible route through which relevant evidence can be detected, connected to the closed question, and brought to someone able to act. The paper assesses provisional closure by whether the specified trigger can be detected, linked to the prior issue, and translated into a feasible step of reopening. It distinguishes retaining these conditions from their subsequent use: storage alone does not ensure monitoring, recognition, authority, or action. It also separates preserving a route back from the later conversion of detected discrepancy into effective revision. The account concerns consequential unresolved dependencies and does not require every conclusion to remain provisional. The mechanism is situated alongside Charles S. Peirce’s account of inquiry as the settlement of doubt and examined through two documented cases. Olympic anti-doping sample storage preserves material for later reanalysis when new information or improved detection methods become available. Japan’s conditional, time-limited approval of HeartSheet required follow-up and reapplication with survival evidence; the submitted analysis did not demonstrate superiority on its primary endpoint, and regular approval was refused. These cases are interpreted through published studies and institutional reports, with attention to the retained evidence, review conditions, and authority required to reopen a settled decision. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who retains and monitors reopening conditions, who can authorize reconsideration, and who bears the continuing cost of maintaining a route back. Potential applications in human–AI research include preserving assumption records, specifying review triggers, routing later evidence to responsible decision makers, and designing processes through which decisions can return to active inquiry.

items.title: ProbMedTOD: A Bayesian Network Guided Task-Oriented Dialogue System for Patient History Taking
items.abstract: Patient history taking is a strategic, multi-turn process that refines diagnostic hypotheses through iterative questioning, mirroring clinical reasoning where each inquiry updates beliefs over candidate diagnoses. Deploying AI in this setting is constrained by privacy, cost, and latency, making Small Language Models (SLMs) a more desirable backbone compared to larger LLMs. However, SLMs capture only the fast, intuitive "System 1" side of this process and lack explicit mechanisms for the deliberative "System 2" reasoning needed to maintain and update diagnostic uncertainty over time. Bayesian Networks (BayesNets) offer a natural complement, providing an interpretable framework for auditable probabilistic belief tracking. Yet, clinical BayesNets are difficult to construct due to their reliance on expert curated structure, dependencies, and parameters. We introduce ProbMedTOD, which automatically synthesizes a clinical BayesNet from a small number of clinical notes in three stages: ontology building, structure prediction, and parameter estimation. ProbMedTOD then integrates the resulting BayesNet with SLMs, enabling probabilistic reasoning in multi-turn dialogues. A BayesNet Agent maintains real-time posterior distributions over diagnoses, while a Policy Agent picks diagnostically informative questions. Experiments on DDXPlus and MIMIC-IV Notes show that ProbMedTOD outperforms LLM-only and retrieval-based baselines, with especially strong gains for smaller models.

items.title: Process Before Prompting: A Pedagogical Framework for Preserving Evaluative Responsibility When Integrating Generative AI into Creative Media Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can expand the range of candidate solutions available during design exploration, but it can also obscure whether students have engaged in the iterative design reasoning and evaluative judgement that studio teaching is intended to develop. This article examines how GenAI can be integrated into creative media education without displacing the cognitive processes through which creative expertise is cultivated. It draws on design research, automation literature, and cognitive load theory, alongside illustrative teaching cases spanning undergraduate and postgraduate animation, visual effects, and game design curricula at Auckland University of Technology and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University. We argue that the educational value of GenAI depends not on the sophistication of its outputs alone, but on whether students retain responsibility for evaluative judgement throughout the design process. We propose Process Before Prompting, a pedagogical framework intended to preserve this responsibility within human-led cycles of divergence, convergence, and appreciative judgement. Students establish an initial creative intention before engaging with GenAI and remain responsible for interpreting, refining, and selecting among both human- and AI-generated candidates. This framework offers practical guidance for scaffolding independent judgement and assessing evidence of iterative design reasoning within existing studio teaching practices.

items.title: Production-source disclosures, higher-order creative attributions, and audience reception of two-dimensional animation: evidence from a randomized source-disclosure experiment
items.abstract: Introduction Attribution theory explains how audiences use observable information to infer otherwise unobservable agents and processes behind creative work. This study applied this perspective to examine how production-source disclosures influence source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience reception of two-dimensional animation. Methods In a randomized experiment, 626 adults were assigned to one of four production-source disclosure conditions—undisclosed, human-made, human–AI collaborative, or AI-led—while viewing the same three animation clips, all of which were actually produced through human–AI collaboration. We examined between-condition differences in source-role perceptions, higher-order creative attributions, and audience-reception outcomes, as well as concurrent associations between higher-order creative attributions and audience reception. Results The disclosures clearly differentiated participants’ perceptions of AI and human involvement. Perceived creative effort was statistically significant before correction but did not meet the α = 0.05 criterion after Holm adjustment ( p = 0.0502); the only corrected contrast indicated lower perceived creative effort in the human–AI collaborative condition than in the human-made condition. No statistically reliable omnibus between-condition differences emerged for perceived authorship, perceived emotional authenticity, artistic evaluation, situational immersion, or viewing and recommendation intention. Higher-order creative attributions were positively associated with all three audience-reception indicators in concurrent analyses, although the strong correlation between perceived emotional authenticity and situational immersion warrants caution about measurement overlap. Discussion The findings indicate that the diagnosticity of a production-source cue depends on the judgment target: the disclosures clearly reorganized perceived production roles but did not yield statistically reliable corresponding differences across most higher-order creative attributions or reception outcomes. The attribution–reception relations represent concurrent covariation rather than causal mediation. Because the three clips were presented in a fixed order, material and order effects cannot be separated, and the equivalence analyses did not establish negligible between-condition differences.

items.title: Proposal of Facial Shiatsu Massage Exergame System with AI-Based Quiz Generator for Smart Healthcare
items.abstract: The World Health Organization (WHO) identifies high blood pressure (hypertension) as a major global public health concern and a significant risk factor for cardiovascular diseases. Therefore, facial Shiatsu massage can be a good solution to alleviate them. However, most people are not only unfamiliar with the locations of acupressure points for proper massage but also lack motivation to conduct it regularly. In this paper, we propose a facial Shiatsu massage exergame system as an effective approach to solve these conditions together. The system runs on a low-cost PC with a camera, provides a simple quiz on a selective topic, and recognizes an answer gesture of a player to select one choice to each question. A generative AI-based quiz generator is implemented to automatically generate quiz questions across different categories providing flexible and varied educational content for the proposed smart healthcare exergame system. An answer gesture is defined for pressing a proper acupressure point with an index finger, which is recognized by applying a MediaPipe library to a user’s face image taken by a PC camera. In this paper, four gestures are implemented to select one of the four choices in each question. For accuracy evaluation, first, we implemented the answer gesture recognition program and investigated the gesture recognition accuracy. Then, for effectiveness evaluation, we implemented the quiz generator using Ollama, produced quizzes on Japanese History, Simple Arithmetic, Indonesian Words, and Taiwan Geography with 50 questions for each topic, and asked 20 persons to use the system. For each user, we measured health condition-related indices such as blood pressure, body temperature, and facial skin moisture level before and after the system use by each person. In addition, we conducted a questionnaire and calculated the Usability and User Experience score. These results indicate the potential feasibility of the proposed system.

items.title: Psychometric Comparison of the NASA-TLX and PROS-TLX for Myoelectric Prosthesis Use
items.abstract: Background: Prosthesis users report high cognitive workload, or the mental effort needed to achieve task performance. The NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) is the most common subjective workload measure. However, it was developed for general human–machine interfaces and may not capture prosthesis-specific demands. The recently proposed Prosthesis Task Load Index (PROS-TLX) includes additional domains relevant to prosthesis use, yet its psychometric properties have not been established. This study compared the convergent validity, test-retest reliability, and measurement error of the NASA-TLX and PROS-TLX across two groups.Methods: Ten individuals without limb difference performed a timed reach-and-grasp task using a myoelectric prosthetic emulator in both a physical and virtual environment. Additionally, ten individuals with upper limb difference performed an accuracy- and time-based activity of daily living using their customary myoelectric, multi-grip prosthesis. Both groups completed two sessions at least a week apart and rated workload using the NASA-TLX and the PROS-TLX in both sessions. Because the PROS-TLX has more total subscales, we modified the scoring of the PROS-TLX to align it with the NASA-TLX. For both surveys, total workload scores were a weighted average of the subscales, ranging from low (0) to high (100). We compared total workload scores between the surveys using Pearson's correlation and calculated the intraclass correlation coefficients, measurement error, and minimum detectable change for each survey. We also explored the role of session number, survey, and task environment on the survey subscales and the relationships between subscales and task performance outcomes.Results: For emulator users, the PROS-TLX and NASA-TLX total workload scores were moderately correlated in session 1 (r>0.63), suggesting good convergent validity. However, for prosthesis users, the surveys were weakly correlated in session 1 (r=0.13). The PROS-TLX demonstrated higher test–retest reliability point estimates (ICC=0.44–0.83) and lower measurement error (SEM=7.43-10.79) than NASA-TLX (ICC=0.18-0.45, SEM=10.52-17.29), though the confidence intervals were large. The prosthesis-specific subscale of uncertainty varied by task environment and correlated with performance outcomes.Conclusions: The PROS-TLX adds prosthesis-specific contributors to workload to the NASA-TLX with higher reliability and lower measurement error estimates, but wide confidence intervals limit conclusions. Larger studies in prosthesis users are needed.

items.title: QPAFusion: Query-Guided Radar Refinement and Prior-Guided Adaptive Fusion for Marine Object Detection
items.abstract: Accurate marine target detection is essential for maritime situational awareness and safe navigation by unmanned surface vehicles. However, uneven radar returns and uncertain spatial correspondence complicate radar–camera fusion, while input-level integration does not explicitly adapt subsequent feature processing to local radar evidence. We propose QPAFusion, which refines multi-scale features through query-guided local radar sampling and adaptively aggregates feature branches using radar priors. On the WaterScenes dataset, QPAFusion achieves 64.5%mAP50−−95 and 90.9%mAP50, exceeding the reported three-frame REVP fusion baseline by 2.0 and 2.1 percentage points, respectively, with mAP50 gains of 6.4 and 3.1 percentage points on the adverse-lighting and adverse-weather subsets. These results support combining local-radar refinement with adaptive feature aggregation for object detection on the water surface, with larger accuracy gains on the evaluated adverse-condition subsets.

items.title: Quality Assurance Framework for AI Governance and Integration in Higher Education Accreditation: A First Operational Model for Safe AI Integration
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming embedded in higher education systems, influencing teaching, assessment, research, and institutional decision-making. Despite the growing adoption of AI, existing governance approaches remain largely principle-based, emphasizing ethical guidelines such as transparency, accountability, and fairness without providing operational mechanisms for implementation within quality assurance (QA) and accreditation systems. This creates a critical gap between AI governance principles and the procedural structures through which educational quality and institutional accountability are evaluated. This study addresses this gap by developing an operational quality assurance framework to systematically integrate AI governance into a ten-step higher education accreditation lifecycle, with explicitly differentiated AI permission levels and defined boundaries for human evaluative authority. Using a conceptual and policy-synthesis approach, the study integrates global AI governance principles, established QA standards, and accreditation practices into a risk-based, human-centered governance model. The framework operationalizes AI governance and integration through a model that defines the role, boundaries, and permissible levels of AI use across each stage of the accreditation process. A central feature of the model is the explicit preservation of human decision-making authority in evaluative and high-stakes accreditation stages. The study reconceptualizes AI integration in higher education as a quality assurance and governance challenge rather than solely a technological innovation problem. By embedding AI governance and integrating it directly within accreditation processes, the proposed model provides a practical bridge between ethical principles and operational implementation. The proposed framework provides a structured basis for quality assurance agencies, regulators, and higher education institutions to consider risk-based AI governance within accreditation processes, with its feasibility, effectiveness, and transferability requiring further evaluation through implementation and empirical validation.

items.title: Quality-controlled synthetic oversampling for imbalanced tabular classification using large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Many tabular classification tasks involve imbalanced classes, but synthetic oversampling can produce rows that violate feature constraints or duplicate existing observations. We present QualSynth, a training-free framework that prompts a large language model to make sparse edits to real minority-class rows under data-derived feature constraints and a machine-readable output contract. A deterministic validation layer checks each candidate’s structure, values, and duplication before admitting it to the training set. We evaluated QualSynth on eight benchmark datasets with ten seeds against four synthetic oversamplers, including the widely used SMOTE, and class-weighted learning without augmentation. QualSynth achieved the highest F1 score among the synthetic oversamplers on four datasets, while SMOTE had the best average ranks. In equivalence tests, QualSynth and SMOTE differed by less than prespecified margins of 0.03 in F1 score and 0.02 in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). After correction for multiple comparisons, the only pairwise difference was higher ROC-AUC for QualSynth than for the diffusion model TabDDPM. Class weighting alone had the best overall ranks, and no augmentation strategy improved aggregate ROC-AUC over the unweighted reference. QualSynth is therefore a controlled, inspectable option for minority-class augmentation, with predictive utility comparable to SMOTE’s.

items.title: RamanGPT maps bidirectionally between crystal structures and Raman spectra of inorganic materials
items.abstract: Raman spectroscopy is one of the most accessible vibrational probes in materials laboratories, but its forward problem (structure to spectrum) is bottlenecked by the cost of density functional perturbation theory, and its inverse problem (spectrum to structure) typically relies on retrieval against curated references. We introduce RamanGPT, a deep-learning framework that addresses both directions for crystalline inorganic materials. The forward model, an Atomistic Line Graph Neural Network (ALIGNN), is trained on the 5,099-material Computational Raman Database and predicts 200-bin spectra over 50–1000 $$\hbox {cm}^{-1}$$ with 53.8% of the 509 held-out materials reaching an active-region cosine similarity of at least 0.354, capturing qualitative features of the target spectrum. The model also shows qualitative agreement with an experimental measurement of metallic 1T $$\hbox {VSe}_{2}$$ , a system absent from the training set. The inverse model fine-tunes DiffractGPT, a large language model already trained for diffraction-to-structure generation, via Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation on Raman-plus-formula prompts, recovering lattice parameters with mean absolute errors of 1.13–2.14 Å and reduced-formula consistency of 92.1% on 508 held-out materials, compared to 17.1% for a formula-conditioned retrieval baseline given identical inputs. A cosine-similarity matcher and an inverse $$\rightarrow$$ relax $$\rightarrow$$ forward consistency loop are deployed at https://atomgpt.org/raman .

items.title: Recreation Perceptions Across Access Settings in Mountainous Linear Cultural Heritage: Evidence from the Great Wall
items.abstract: Mountainous linear cultural heritage corridors include both formal-access and restricted-access sections, but recreation perceptions across these settings remain insufficiently understood. Using 17,034 online reviews from 18 Ming Great Wall sections in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region, China, this study compared perception-element prominence, sentiment orientations, and textual co-occurrence through an integrated analytical framework, LLM-assisted labelling, statistical comparisons, section-level sensitivity analyses, and co-occurrence networks. Embodied recreation was prominent in both settings. Section-level comparisons showed greater attention to management and services, particularly entry costs and infrastructure, in formal-access sections, whereas mountain environments and risk and use impacts were more prominent in restricted-access sections, particularly naturalness and heritage preservation. Although sentiment profiles differed descriptively, no section-level sentiment comparisons remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Co-occurrence analysis revealed associations between infrastructure and embodied recreation in formal-access reviews, while restricted-access reviews linked heritage preservation, mountain environments, bodily activity, and safety concerns. By extending recreation-perception analysis beyond formally managed attractions, this study provides comparative evidence of shared recreational interests and differentiated management concerns within a continuous heritage corridor. The findings inform access-sensitive management and corridor-scale heritage conservation, subject to limitations associated with platform coverage and reviewer self-selection.

items.title: Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models
items.abstract: Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. Local probabilistic robustness addresses the behavioural variation hidden when different concrete inputs are treated as the same task. Published findings and an illustrative customer-support example motivate the roadmap; its integrated validation remains an open research task. Reliability claims complement, but do not replace, separate safety and security arguments. Capability scores should therefore be complemented by versioned operational claims that state whose requirements are covered, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty.

items.title: Responding Fairly: Integrating Critical Controls, Incident Investigation and Human Factors to Strengthen Organisational Learning
items.abstract: Background: High-potential incidents in construction are often initially understood through the actions of the person closest to the event. This can narrow investigations, obscure the operational and organisational conditions that shaped performance, and weaken both learning and trust. As HEB Construction’s Critical Control Management programme matured, the organisation identified a disconnect between its prevention approach and the way incidents, individual actions and accountability were considered. Aim: This practice case study describes the development and implementation of Responding Fairly, an approach intended to connect Critical Control Management, Incident Cause Analysis Method investigations, Human and Organisational Performance principles, and people processes. Its purpose is to support fair, consistent and evidence-informed decisions while maintaining accountability. Approach: Rather than introducing a separate process, HEB aligned existing investigation, critical control and people practices around a shared sequence of questions. Investigations first consider which controls should have prevented the event, whether those controls were present and effective, how the work was designed and supported, and which conditions influenced decisions at the time. Individual actions are considered after this context has been established. The approach is jointly supported by Operations, Health and Safety, and Human Resources, with leader coaching and practical guidance used to strengthen consistency. Practice example and findings: A service-strike investigation showed how an apparent failure by an operator was better understood when outdated plans, a changed work scope, conflicting site markings, unavailable technical support and time pressure were examined together. This broader analysis led to strengthened service verification requirements, revalidation following scope changes and clearer excavation controls. Early implementation experience indicates richer learning, more targeted corrective actions, greater leader confidence and improved worker perceptions of fairness. Conclusion: Responding Fairly demonstrates how prevention, investigation and accountability can be treated as one connected learning system. Context does not remove accountability; it enables accountability to be located more fairly and supported by fuller evidence. The experience also suggests that a framework alone is insufficient: leaders require capability, support and confidence to pause, tolerate uncertainty and understand the conditions surrounding an event before reaching conclusions.

items.title: Responsive Cues Converted Into Reciprocal Obligation: When Something That Answers Seems to Be Owed, or to Owe
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Responsive Cues Converted Into Reciprocal Obligation, a mechanism through which repeated signs of attention can lead someone to feel that care is owed in either direction. A device that comes when called or asks to be held may come to seem like a companion who depends on its owner. The owner, in turn, may expect someone to keep that companion functioning. The mechanism concerns the point at which such an expectation extends beyond any commitment established by the people or institutions behind the device. The paper places this account alongside Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass’s work on how people apply social conventions to computers and other media. It asks what a particular person came to expect, which words or actions connect that expectation to a responsive cue, and who undertook to honor it. A person’s account of companionship can establish what the relationship meant to them. A provider’s statements and policies supply evidence about what that provider promised. Sony’s AIBO illustrates the distinction. Sony offered repairs for its earlier models for stated periods, and its repair clinic operated beyond the latest deadline in its notice. In 2018, owners of the new aibo asked Sony to extend its policy of providing repairs for seven years after withdrawal from sale. The founder of A FUN, an independent repair firm, argued that Sony bore continuing responsibility for the companion it had brought to market. The paper leaves the merits of that demand open. GROOVE X’s LOVOT provides a contrast through priced care plans whose written terms specify what the maker will cover. Part of the Presence Through Technology series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a way to examine expectations of discretion in human–AI interaction. A conversational assistant might recall a private concern and ask about it weeks later. If the user explains that being remembered led them to expect the exchange to stay private, that account connects a specific cue to a specific expectation. The provider’s confidentiality commitments can then be compared with what the user understood.

items.title: Revocation Window in RAG: Quantifying Unauthorized Retrieval Exposure During Access-Control Propagation
items.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems often store document chunks in a vector index together with a copy of their access-control metadata. When a user's permission is revoked in the authoritative permission store, this indexed copy may remain stale, allowing the vector database to keep returning protected content. This paper measures the duration of this revocation window and separates two outcomes: unauthorized index retrieval, in which the vector database returns a protected chunk, and LLM-context exposure, in which that chunk reaches the context assembled for the language model. We built a controlled synthetic testbed with PostgreSQL as the authoritative permission store and Qdrant as the vector index, and evaluated six enforcement configurations: periodic synchronization, event-driven synchronization, a no-worker control, query-time authorization, hybrid authorization, and query-time authorization with a 10-second decision cache. Each configuration retained 27 trials (5 for the control) within a 35-second observation window. The median context-level revocation propagation time was 9.92 s for 20-second periodic synchronization, 14 ms for event-driven synchronization, and 4.98 s for the cached query-time configuration. Under periodic synchronization, 87.7% of relevant queries placed the protected chunk in the context before revocation was enforced. Query-time and hybrid authorization blocked protected content at the first post-revocation probe (0 ms at probe resolution) even though the stale index kept returning it, while the no-worker control never achieved stable enforcement within the window. These findings describe the tested synthetic testbed and are not production guarantees.

items.title: Revolutionizing healthcare through AI: A systematic review of applications and impacts
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a technology with tremendous potential to revolutionize healthcare, contributing to progress in medical diagnostics, clinical decision support, personalized medicine, patient monitoring, medical research, and healthcare management. This systematic review covers the current use of AI in healthcare, its clinical effects and hindrances for implementation. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines were followed to conduct a systematic literature search. The search query was conducted in major electronic databases using specific keywords of the studies and results, such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and other sources, including studies on artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, large language models, healthcare applications, clinical decision support, medical imaging, drug discovery, digital health, and healthcare data systems. This evidence review identifies evidence of how AI is being used in a variety of healthcare areas such as medical imaging and diagnostics, virtual patient monitoring, drug design, precision medicine, rehabilitation, patient engagement, and operational health care processes. The use of AI has been shown to have the potential to enhance the accuracy of diagnosis, improve clinical decision‐making, personalize care, and optimize healthcare workflows. However, there are substantial hurdles to overcome, such as data privacy and security issues, algorithmic bias, the lack of the clinical validation of AI models, regulatory scrutiny, infrastructure challenges, and the need for effective clinical validation. The key takeaways from this review are the need for a balanced approach to the integration of AI in healthcare, acknowledging both the technological innovations and the ethical, regulatory, and human factors considerations that need to be addressed. More large‐scale clinical validation studies are needed as well as the establishment of reliable AI systems and strategies to ensure responsible and fair use of AI in healthcare.

items.title: Risk Factor Analysis of Bridge Operation and Maintenance Safety Accidents Based on Text Mining
items.abstract: To effectively prevent bridge operation and maintenance (O&M) accidents, a hybrid method integrating text mining with Bayesian network theory was adopted to systematically analyze the causal factors of accidents affecting bridge O&M safety and their interrelationships. First, text mining techniques were applied to preprocess data from 226 Chinese bridge O&M accident cases (1999–2025). Using the BERTopic topic modeling approach, 20 safety risk topics were identified, and 20 corresponding causal factors were extracted based on key feature words under these topics. Drawing on the Human‐Machine‐Environment‐Management safety management theory, the safety risk causal factors were classified into four risk categories, namely, bridge self‐factors, O&M environmental factors, human factors, and management defects. The Apriori algorithm was employed to analyze the interrelationships among risk factors, from which a total of 42 strong association rules were extracted; these rules were then taken as the basis for constructing a Bayesian network model. Through Bayesian network reasoning and sensitivity analysis, the key causal factors, sensitive factors, and the maximum‐probability causal chain of bridge O&M safety accidents were clarified. Analysis of the key causal chain revealed that the chain with the highest probability of leading to bridge O&M safety accidents is as follows: inadequate industrial supervision→substandard construction quality→structural construction defects→insufficient structural bearing capacity→bridge accidents. Sensitivity analysis identified vessel collision and floating debris collision as the key sensitive factors influencing bridge O&M safety accidents, whereas insufficient structural bearing capacity and other relevant factors were defined as moderately sensitive factors, thus providing a robust basis for the targeted prevention and control of such accidents. This method avoids the interference of experts' subjective factors, conducts an in‐depth analysis of bridge O&M safety accidents based on objective data, and provides theoretical support and methodological guidance for formulating more scientific accident prevention measures, which endows it with important practical significance in bridge engineering practice.

items.title: Risk Stratification for 7-Day Mortality After ICU Admission Using General-Purpose Large Language Models and Structured Electronic Health Records: Predictive Performance and Reasoning Alignment Across Three Cohorts
items.abstract: Background Early risk stratification after intensive care unit (ICU) admission may inform treatment intensity, goals-of-care discussions, and resource allocation. Developing and maintaining supervised machine learning models requires large labelled cohorts and technical infrastructure that may not be available in all settings. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) can generate risk estimates with human-readable rationales, but their performance and reasoning quality across independent healthcare systems remain uncertain. Methods We analysed three ICU cohorts: eICU-CRD (208 US hospitals), MIMIC-IV (US), and a Korean tertiary-hospital subset of K-MIMIC (Korea). Seven-day mortality after ICU admission was predicted from routinely collected demographic, laboratory, and vital sign variables recorded during the first 24 hours. Six supervised machine learning and deep learning models were developed in eICU-CRD and externally validated in MIMIC-IV and K-MIMIC. GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro were evaluated with four prompting strategies in 2,000-stay samples per cohort, without cohort-specific training or task-specific fine-tuning. Clinical concepts mentioned in GPT-5 rationales were compared with patient-level predictor importance from an XGBoost reference model; two clinicians rated 150 rationales for clinical trustworthiness. Results Analyses included 124,020, 84,926, and 6,673 ICU stays. Among supervised models, the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.936 for XGBoost in the held-out eICU-CRD set, 0.858 for the multilayer perceptron in MIMIC-IV, and 0.957 for XGBoost in K-MIMIC. In the corresponding 2,000-stay LLM evaluation samples, GPT-5 achieved AUROCs of 0.925, 0.822, and 0.926, respectively, but generally had a lower area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC) and, at evaluated operating thresholds, lower specificity. Overlap with the five most influential concepts was partial (precision, 0.47; recall, 0.55), but mentioned concepts had greater mean patient-level importance than nonmentioned concepts in 98.1% of patients (P < 0.001). Clinician-rated trustworthiness averaged 4.03 ± 0.63 on a 5-point scale, with ratings within one point in 83% of cases. Conclusions Supervised models generally achieved the highest discrimination for 7-day mortality after ICU admission. GPT-5 achieved high discrimination without cohort-specific training or task-specific fine-tuning, and its patient-specific rationales preferentially referenced influential predictors and received favorable clinician ratings. Prospective evaluation of reasoning faithfulness and clinical utility is required before clinical use.

items.title: RustC 4 ++: Improving Rust Code-Comment Inconsistency Detection via Hybrid LLM and Static Analysis
items.abstract: Maintaining consistency between source code and its associated comments is essential for software reliability, maintainability, and user experience, particularly in the Rust programming ecosystem, where comments serve as both developer guidance and an authoritative API contract. However, existing automated inconsistency detection approaches are largely tailored for object-oriented languages and fall short of addressing Rust’s unique features, such as explicit panic semantics, trait-based abstraction, and idiomatic use of option and finiteness constraints. In this article, we introduce RustC 4 ++, a novel hybrid framework that integrates large language model (LLM)-driven constraint extraction, static program analysis, and SMT-based bidirectional verification to detect and diagnose code-comment inconsistencies in Rust. RustC 4 ++ extends previous solutions by supporting a richer taxonomy of constraints, including interval, boundary, existence, option, and finiteness constraints, and pioneers a systematic method for propagating comment constraints across trait and implementation boundaries. Leveraging chain-of-thought prompt engineering, RustC 4 ++ robustly interprets natural language comments, maps it to formal specifications, and checks their alignment with code logic through precise static analysis and formal reasoning. We conduct extensive experiments on 17 diverse, real-world Rust projects, demonstrating that RustC 4 ++ substantially outperforms prior tools in both precision and recall, and is capable of uncovering subtle, actionable inconsistencies that have led to confirmed fixes in upstream repositories. By elevating comments to enforceable, verifiable contracts, RustC 4 ++ not only enhances code quality and comment reliability in the Rust ecosystem but also offers generalizable techniques and insights for automated code comment analysis in other modern programming languages.

items.title: S-Eval : Towards Automated Safety Evaluation with Enhancement for Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing with their transformative and emergent capabilities. However, recent evidence indicates that LLMs can produce harmful content that violates social norms, raising significant concerns regarding the safety ramifications of deploying these advanced models. Thus, it is both critical and imperative to perform a rigorous and comprehensive safety evaluation of LLMs before deployment. Despite this need, owing to the extensiveness of LLM generation space, it still lacks a unified and standardized risk taxonomy to systematically reflect the LLM content safety, automated assessment techniques to explore the potential risks efficiently, as well as defense mechanisms for timely mitigation. To bridge the striking gap, we propose S-Eval , a novel LLM-based automated S afety Eval uation framework. S-Eval incorporates three key components, i.e., an expert testing LLM \(\mathcal{M}_{t}\) , a novel safety critique LLM \(\mathcal{M}_{c}\) , and constitutional defense. The expert testing LLM \(\mathcal{M}_{t}\) is responsible for automatically generating test cases in accordance with the proposed risk management (including 8 risk dimensions and a total of 102 subdivided risks). The safety critique LLM \(\mathcal{M}_{c}\) can provide quantitative and explainable safety evaluations for better risk awareness of LLMs. Furthermore, the constitutional defense enables differentiated safety constraints in a non-intrusive manner. In contrast to prior works, S-Eval differs in significant ways: (i) efficient— we construct a multi-dimensional and open-ended benchmark comprising 220,000 test cases across 102 risks utilizing \(\mathcal{M}_{t}\) and conduct safety evaluations for 29 influential LLMs via \(\mathcal{M}_{c}\) on our benchmark. The entire process is fully automated and requires no human involvement. (ii) effective— extensive validations show that S-Eval facilitates a more thorough assessment and better perception of potential LLM risks, where \(\mathcal{M}_{c}\) not only accurately quantifies the risks of LLMs but also provides explainable and in-depth insights into their safety, and our constitutional defense method can effectively mitigate the safety risks. (iii) adaptive— S -Eval can be flexibly configured and adapted to the rapid evolution of LLMs and accompanying new safety threats, test generation methodologies, safety critique approaches, and defense mechanisms. We further study the impacts of hyperparameters, languages, and reasoning on model safety, which may lead to promising directions for future research. S-Eval has been deployed at our industrial partner, Alibaba Group, for automated safety evaluation of multiple LLMs serving millions of users, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world scenarios.

items.title: Safety in Design Through University–Industry Collaboration: Embedding Ergonomics in Aviation Product Development. Air NZ AUT Joint Projects
items.abstract: Problem: Safety-in-design decisions are often made before users, operating environments and manual-handling demands are understood. This risks products valued by customers creating avoidable physical demands for staff who handle them. Air New Zealand is collaborating with Auckland University of Technology (AUT) to embed human factors and ergonomics (HFE) in product development. Method: The collaboration engages students from second year to Masters level in manual-handling risk assessment, the hierarchy of controls and ergonomic principles. Students examine products and processes as systems through site-based problem framing, worker input, task analysis and concept review. Two case studies: adaptation of an airline jug, and redesign of the Business Premier mattress. The mattress project, led with a Bachelor of Industrial Design student, mapped its lifecycle: laundry, supply and amenities placement, transport to the aircraft, cabin-crew interaction, storage, offboarding and return to laundry. Whilst second year students did the same with the coffee jug.

items.title: Same Rank, Different Needs: Rethinking LoRA Redistribution in Federated Learning
items.abstract: Federated low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables clients with different resource budgets to collaboratively fine-tune foundation models. To distribute an aggregated update within each client's rank budget, existing methods commonly retain its leading singular directions. However, directions that best reconstruct the update matrix need not best preserve its responses on a particular client's inputs: a lower-energy direction may matter more to that recipient. We formalize this mismatch and show that matrix-optimal truncation can incur arbitrarily larger response error than another readout of the same rank. Motivated by this result, we propose Receiver-Aware Subspace Adaptation (RASA), a plug-in framework for receiver-aware knowledge transfer. RASA uses compact diagonal input second moments to perform uncentered PCA of receiver-weighted update responses. The resulting readout is globally optimal for the rank-constrained receiver objective and preserves at least as much response energy as spectral truncation under the diagonal metric. RASA also introduces spectral-reference aggregation, which removes the personalized initialization offset while retaining the locally learned increment. Experiments on DomainNet-100, NICO++, GLUE, and SuperNI demonstrate RASA's effectiveness across methods under resource, task, and data heterogeneity. In particular, RASA improves DomainNet-100 accuracy by 3.23 percentage points with FlexLoRA and achieves gains of up to 8.33 ROUGE-L points on seen SuperNI tasks and 4.37 on unseen tasks with modest overhead.

items.title: SCAFFOLD: Toward Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport for Reusable LLM-Agent Skills
items.abstract: An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. We argue that the appropriate unit of prospective trust is a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC): a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters. The paper sharpens this position through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence remains admissible after context change. It distinguishes evidence admissibility from truth of the supported safety or effectiveness claim; states a conditional preservation result and its limits; specifies three-valued applicability and asymmetric context-transfer judgments; and illustrates how provenance dependence and policy-invalidating changes alter authorization. We explicitly relate the proposal to assurance cases, contracts, and skill-library maintenance rather than claiming novelty for their ingredients. A falsifiable longitudinal evaluation would compare WRC-guided policies with strong version-aware baselines at matched coverage, utility, and review cost. This paper contributes a formalized problem statement, testable design obligations, and reporting protocol, not an implemented verifier, empirical superiority result, or proof of universal agent safety.

items.title: School leaders’ perspectives on teachers’ AI experiences and leadership support in South Asian schools
items.abstract: Schools across Asia are experiencing rapid educational change due to technology integration. Teachers increasingly face pressure to use Artificial Intelligence (AI), while also worrying about errors, cheating, ethical concerns, and unclear institutional policies. This study explored school leaders’ perceptions of how teachers experience AI-related anxiety and how leadership practices support teachers’ AI competence in South Asian countries. A phenomenological research design was employed. Using purposive and snowball sampling, 10 high school leaders from Pakistan, Sri Lanka, India, Bangladesh, and Nepal were selected. Data were collected online through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Four themes emerged from the findings. First, school leaders perceived that teachers feared accountability and public criticism when AI-generated outputs were inaccurate or inappropriate. Second, school leaders reported that teachers expressed concerns about cheating, fairness, and loss of professional identity. Third, school leaders described reducing teachers’ anxiety by creating low-risk professional learning environments and encouraging peer support. Fourth, leaders established clear guidance regarding acceptable AI use, transparency, and student data protection. Across the participating schools, leaders consistently viewed teachers’ AI-related anxiety as a major barrier to responsible AI adoption. The findings suggest that leadership practices supporting ethical AI governance, collaborative professional learning, and equitable AI implementation contribute to sustainable teacher professional development and responsible educational transformation.

items.title: SCOPE: A lightweight-training LLM framework for air traffic control readback monitoring
items.abstract: Pilot readback of Air Traffic Control (ATC) voice instructions is a primary safeguard against miscommunication in air transportation. However, readback anomalies remain implicated in approximately 80% of aviation incidents. This vulnerability is further exacerbated by rising traffic volume and elevated cognitive workload, thereby motivating automated readback monitoring by machine. Traditional rule-based and machine learning approaches struggle to generalize across the highly variable and evolving phraseology of air traffic controller-pilot communications. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have opened a new avenue through their strong reasoning and generalization capabilities, existing approaches still face deployment and computational barriers in practice. In this work, we propose Semantic reasoning for Communication via Open-set Plug-in with Examples (SCOPE), a novel lightweight-training LLM framework that advances both the efficiency and accuracy of machine-based ATC readback monitoring. The core idea is to couple a plug-in open-set classifier with a carefully designed in-context learning mechanism on top of a frozen LLM. Extensive experiments on the semi-synthetic communication dataset show that SCOPE attains superior accuracy while delivering the low-latency response required for operational environments. Under a few-shot setting, SCOPE achieves 91.05% accuracy in open-set detection and corrects 96.63% of anomalous readbacks, thereby outperforming the strongest available baselines while providing explanations for its decisions. These findings demonstrate the potential of our framework as a practical pathway toward interpretable and controllable ATC readback monitoring.

items.title: Self-Driving Universities: An Autonomous, Formally Verified Multi-Agent Framework for Dynamic Curriculum and Resource Optimization
items.abstract: University timetabling and resource allocation automation has historically relied on rigid operations research models that scale poorly during sudden operational disruptions. While recent advances in multi-agent systems (MASs) and large language models (LLMs) offer dynamic semantic adaptability, these purely probabilistic architectures fail to satisfy strict, NP-hard combinatorial constraints, rendering them unsafe for independent administrative execution. This research introduces a hybrid agentic-symbolic framework that bridges this evaluation gap by decoupling neural reasoning from deterministic execution. The architecture utilizes a network of specialized LLM agents to negotiate institutional demand. Meanwhile, a Z3 formal verification engine acts as an immutable gatekeeper, mathematically blocking any physically impossible schedule from executing. To evaluate hardware feasibility, the framework underwent an 8-semester longitudinal simulation across two distinct institutional topologies (totaling 16 simulated semesters) across heterogeneous computing environments, incorporating stochastic structural and personnel shocks. Empirical telemetry indicates a critical failure mode within constrained 23 Edge CPU infrastructure, which we characterize as autoregressive token explosion, in which 24 generative model’s attention mechanism collapses during the production of large schemas, paralyzing the system. To address this, the architecture substitutes conventional substantial solvers with a sub-millisecond greedy heuristic fallback. The results demonstrate that this deterministic safety mechanism intercepts catastrophic neural failures and resolves the scheduling matrix in under 1.0 millisecond. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that formally verified multi-agent systems can attain zero-violation compliance and uninterrupted institutional continuity when supported by lightweight, hardware-aware heuristic overrides.

items.title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
items.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels.We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2,000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content.We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

items.title: Separation of Diagnostic Revision Depths: What Kind of Thing a Failure Asks to Be Reconsidered
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Separation of Diagnostic Revision Depths, a distinction among four ways to investigate a failed expectation. An inquirer can adjust a value within the current model, reopen a condition previously treated as settled, expand the model’s boundary to include an omitted factor, or revise its account of how one quantity or event depends on another. Each operation holds different things fixed. A value that brings a prediction into agreement with an observation establishes that the model can fit that observation at that value. The assumptions retained in making the adjustment still require their own grounds. The paper assesses a diagnosis by asking what evidence supports the chosen revision and what competing revisions would predict. The four operations can overlap or occur in different orders. A small adjustment may have the strongest support. The paper places this distinction alongside Imre Lakatos’s account of research programs, narrowing the question to what a particular response to a single discrepancy can establish. Two historical cases give the distinction concrete form. To explain the anomalous advance of Mercury’s perihelion, Urbain Le Verrier proposed an unseen planet or smaller bodies, Asaph Hall proposed changing the exponent in the law of gravitation, and Albert Einstein accounted for the advance using a new theory of gravitation. In the Mars case, Johannes Kepler adjusted a circular model to fit Tycho Brahe’s observations of planetary positions at opposition. A check against distances exposed a further difficulty. After correction, some predicted positions missed the observations by as much as eight minutes of arc, beyond their estimated precision of two minutes. This gave Kepler grounds to reopen the assumption of circular motion. He subsequently adopted an ellipse. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the distinction has a prospective application in human–AI evaluation. When an AI forecast underestimates a project’s duration, a reviewer might adjust a task estimate, check whether a promised input arrived, include an omitted approval, or revise which tasks the model treats as able to run in parallel. The project record can help the reviewer decide which change the evidence supports.
